blocks.text: I can identify the meaning and the correct pronunciation of homonyms based on their context.

items.title: {homonyms}
items.sub: same spelling, different meaning

items.title: {context}
items.sub: the words around a word give us clues

items.title: community and leisure
items.sub: two curriculum words

blocks.text: Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: Words that have the same spelling as other words but a different meaning. Sometimes they are pronounced differently too.
Words that sound the same, but have different spellings and meanings.
The different types of words that are used to form sentences.
The surrounding words or sentences that help determine the meaning of a word or phrase.

blocks.text: The word homophone comes from Greek. ‘Homos’ means ‘one and the same’ and ‘phon’ means ‘sound’. So homophones have the same sound.
Homophones sound the same, but they have different spellings and different meanings.

items: Learning from the {past} can help us to prepare for the future.
Mr Jones waved as he {passed} me on his bike.

blocks.label: past or passed?
blocks.text: **past** is about things that happened previously in time. **passed** is a past tense verb: going past someone. They sound the same, but the spellings and meanings are different.
The word homonym comes from Greek too. ‘Nym’ means ‘word’ or ‘name’, so homonym means ‘same word’ or ‘same name’.
Homonyms have the {same spelling} as other words, but different meanings. Sometimes they are pronounced differently too.

items.title: The dog began to {bark}.
items.sub: a verb: to bark

items.title: The {bark} of a tree.
items.sub: a noun: the bark on a tree

blocks.q: Tap a pair, then tap the column it belongs in.

items.text: bark (of a dog) / bark (of a tree)
match (a game) / match (to light a fire)
tear (from an eye) / tear (a piece of paper)

blocks.text: The word {match} is a homonym. Look at the different meanings it can have.

items.title: a football {match}
items.sub: Will you come and watch my football match next week?

items.title: colours that {match}
items.sub: The colours in your outfit match perfectly.

items.title: a {match} for a fire
items.sub: We need to find a match to light the fire.

blocks.text: The context and position within a sentence tells us the meaning of the homonym.
The word {tear} is a homonym that can be pronounced in two ways.

items.title: A single {tear} rolled down my cheek.
items.sub: makes the /ear/ sound

items.title: If you {tear} the paper in half, we can each have a piece.
items.sub: makes the /air/ sound

blocks.label: How do we know which way to say it?
blocks.text: The context, and the position of the word in the sentence, tells us how to pronounce it.

blocks.q: Use the context to decide how to say the word.

items.q: ‘A tear ran down her face.’ How is ‘tear’ pronounced?
‘Be careful not to tear your coat.’ How is ‘tear’ pronounced?
‘Yesterday I read a whole chapter.’ How is ‘read’ said here?
‘Please read the sign.’ How is ‘read’ said here?

blocks.text: ‘Read’ in the past tense sounds like ‘red’, the colour. Watch out for that one!
These homonyms are spelt the same and they sound the same, however you use them. Only the meaning changes.

items.title: {scale}
items.sub: to climb a building, or a scale to weigh something on

items.title: {rose}
items.sub: a flower, or ‘I rose from my chair’

items.title: {saw}
items.sub: ‘I saw you’, or a saw to cut through wood

items.title: {fair}
items.sub: a fair coming to town, or ‘that is not fair’

blocks.text: These homonyms are spelt the same, but can be pronounced differently and have different meanings.

items.title: {wind}
items.sub: the wind that blew, or ‘I had to wind it up’

items.title: {wound}
items.sub: a wound in battle, or ‘I wound it up’

items.title: {read}
items.sub: ‘I read the page’, or ‘you must read it’

items.title: {tear}
items.sub: a tear from the eye, or to tear paper

items.title: {bow}
items.sub: can be said in different ways

blocks.text: Unlike many spelling rules, there are no patterns for homonyms and homophones. We just have to learn them, and use the context to know which meaning is which.
The meaning and word class of a homonym can be worked out from its context. Homonyms can be nouns, verbs or adjectives.

items.title: I travelled by {train}.
items.sub: a noun: the thing you travel on

items.title: I am going to {train} hard today.
items.sub: a verb: something you do

blocks.label: Can a homonym belong to different word classes?
blocks.text: Yes. The word ‘train’ can be both a noun and a verb, depending on the context.

blocks.q: Use the context to decide the word class of the word before the colon.

items.text: saw: The gardener used a saw to cut the branch.
saw: I saw you at the shops.
wound: The doctor cleaned the wound.
wound: She wound the wool into a ball.
scale: Put the fruit on the scale.

blocks.text: After flying the kite, Sam carefully wound the string in. You would wind some string up, you wouldn’t get a wound in it. So the context tells us this is the verb ‘wound’, the act of winding something up.

blocks.q: Which meaning of the word in bold fits the sentence?

items.q: The nurse put a plaster on the **wound**.
options: the act of winding something up

items.q: Dad **wound** the string onto a stick.
options: the act of winding something up

items.q: Mum struck a **match** to light the campfire.
options: a thing you strike to start a fire

blocks.text: Now for two words to learn by heart.

items.title: co{mm}unity
items.sub: a group of people living together

items.title: leis{ure}
items.sub: your free time when you are not working

items: **community** has a double m, which can be hard to remember.
**leisure** has the letters ‘ei’ in the middle, which is a rare spelling. It ends in s-u-r-e, so you can remember there is ‘sure’ in leisure.
Two or more words that are spelt the same but have different meanings are called **homonyms**.
Some homonyms are spelt the same but have contrasting sounds and different meanings, like tear, wind, wound or read.
The context of a sentence helps us work out the meaning and the word class of a homonym.
Homophones sound the same, but have different spellings and meanings.

flashcards.back:
A word with the same spelling as another word but a different meaning. Some homonyms are pronounced differently too.

Example: tear, wind, wound, read.

Words that sound the same, but have different spellings and meanings.

Example: hear / here.
Homophones. They sound the same but are spelt differently and have different meanings.

flashcards.front: ‘The dog began to bark.’ and ‘the bark of a tree’. What do we call the word bark?
flashcards.back: A homonym: the same spelling, but different meanings. In the first it is a verb, in the second it is a noun.

flashcards.front: What helps us work out the meaning of a homonym?
flashcards.back: The context: the surrounding words or sentences.

flashcards.front: Give three meanings of the homonym ‘match’.
flashcards.back: A football match, colours that match, and a match to light a fire.

flashcards.front: How is ‘tear’ said in ‘A single tear rolled down my cheek’ and in ‘If you tear the paper’?
flashcards.back: First: the /ear/ sound. Second: the /air/ sound.

flashcards.front: Name four homonyms that sound the same however you use them.
Name homonyms that can be pronounced in different ways.
What word class is ‘train’ in ‘I travelled by train’, and in ‘I am going to train hard today’?
flashcards.back: A noun in the first sentence, a verb in the second.

flashcards.front: How does ‘read’ sound in the past tense?
flashcards.back: Like ‘red’, the colour. Aisha read the instructions carefully.

flashcards.front: Is there a spelling pattern that helps with homonyms and homophones?
flashcards.back: No. We just need to learn them and use the context to work out their meaning.

flashcards.front: Spell the word for a group of people living together.
flashcards.back:
community

Watch out for the double m.

flashcards.front: Spell the word for your free time when you are not working.
flashcards.back:
leisure

The ‘ei’ is a rare spelling. There is ‘sure’ in leisure.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: Spelling homonyms
worksheet.instructions: Read each sentence carefully and use the context to help you. Type your answer as a single word (or as instructed).

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence with the homonym for the drop that rolls down a cheek: He wiped a ___ away as the train departed.
questions.explanation: A tear from the eye. The same spelling is also used for tear (to rip paper), but the context tells us the meaning.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence with the homonym that means an injury: The doctor used a clean bandage to dress the ___.
questions.explanation: A wound is an injury. It is spelt the same as ‘wound’ (winding something up) but is said differently.

questions.prompt: Complete the instruction with the homonym that means to pair things that go together: ___ each sentence to its correct answer.
questions.explanation: To match things is to pair them up. The word match also names a football game and a thing you strike to light a fire.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence with the past tense of the verb ‘to read’: The novel was gripping, so I ___ it in one sitting.
questions.explanation: The past tense is spelt ‘read’ and sounds like the colour ‘red’. The context (‘so I ... it in one sitting’) shows it is past tense.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence with the homonym for a flower: Despite the bad weather, one beautiful ___ grew.
questions.explanation: A rose is a flower you might find in the garden. ‘Rose’ can also be a verb, as in ‘the mountain rose above the clouds’.

questions.prompt: In ‘If you tear the paper in half’, does ‘tear’ sound like ‘ear’ or like ‘air’? Write ear or air.
questions.explanation: Here tear means to rip, and it makes the /air/ sound. (In ‘a single tear rolled down my cheek’ it makes the /ear/ sound.)

questions.prompt: What word class is ‘train’ in the sentence ‘I am going to train hard today’? Write noun or verb.
questions.explanation: It is something you do, so it is a verb. In ‘I travelled by train’ it is a noun.

questions.prompt: What word class is ‘wound’ in the sentence ‘The soldier suffered a serious wound during the battle’? Write noun or verb.
questions.explanation: A wound is an injury: a thing, so it is a noun.

questions.prompt: Spell the word for a group of people living together. It has a double m.
questions.explanation: community: com-mu-ni-ty, with a double m.

questions.prompt: Spell the word for your free time when you are not working. It has ‘ei’ in the middle and ends in s-u-r-e.
questions.explanation: leisure: the ‘ei’ is a rare spelling, and there is ‘sure’ in leisure.

steps.title: Warm-up, goal and key words
doThis: Read the goal together, then look at the four key words: homonym, homophone, word class and context.
Ask the student what each word might mean before showing the meaning.
Recall the strategy for practising spellings: look, cover, write, check.
steps.say: I can identify the meaning and the correct pronunciation of homonyms based on their context.

keywords.meaning: Words that have the same spelling as other words but a different meaning. Sometimes they are pronounced differently too.
words that sound the same, but have different spellings and meanings
different types of words that are used to form sentences
the surrounding words or sentences that help determine the meaning of a word or phrase

checkFor.ask: What is the context of a word?
checkFor.lookFor: The surrounding words or sentences that help determine the meaning of a word or phrase.

recap: Our goal: I can identify the meaning and the correct pronunciation of homonyms based on their context.
Homonyms are spelt the same as other words but have a different meaning. The context is the surrounding words that help us decide which meaning it is.

steps.title: Homophones and homonyms
doThis: Explain that homophones are words that sound the same but have different spellings and different meanings, such as hear and here.
Explain that homonyms are words that have the same spelling as other words but different meanings, such as bark (a dog barking) and bark (on a tree).
Ask whether hear and here are homophones or homonyms, and why.
keyIdeas: Homophones are words that sound the same, but have different spellings and meanings.
Two or more words that are spelt the same but have different meanings are called homonyms.
examples: hear and here are homophones: they sound the same but are spelt differently and have different meanings.
past and passed are homophones: past is about things that happened previously in time, and passed is a past tense verb meaning going past someone.
bark is a homonym: 'The dog began to bark' (a verb) and 'the bark of a tree' (a noun) are spelt the same but have different meanings.

checkFor.ask: Are hear and here homophones or homonyms, and why?
checkFor.lookFor: Homophones: they sound the same but are spelt differently and have different meanings. They are not homonyms because they are not spelt the same.

recap: Homophones sound the same but are spelt differently, like hear and here.
Homonyms are spelt the same but have different meanings, like the bark of a tree and a dog beginning to bark.

steps.title: Using context to find the meaning
doThis: Show that match is a homonym with three meanings: a football match, colours that match, and a match to light a fire.
Explain that the context and position within a sentence tell us the meaning of a homonym.
Show that a homonym can belong to different word classes: train is a noun in 'I travelled by train' and a verb when it means to train hard today.
keyIdeas: The meaning and word class of homonyms can be determined by their context.
Homonyms can be nouns, verbs or adjectives.

keywords.meaning: the surrounding words or sentences that help determine the meaning of a word or phrase
different types of words that are used to form sentences

examples: match: a football match, colours that match, and a match to light a fire.
train: 'I travelled by train' (a noun, the thing you travel on) and to train hard today (a verb, something you do).
scale: 'Measure the ingredients on the scale' (a noun) and 'We must scale the hill' (a verb, the act of climbing up).
rose: 'The mountain rose above the clouds' (a verb) and 'I picked a beautiful rose in the garden' (a noun, a flower).

checkFor.ask: When train means to train hard today, is it a noun or a verb?
checkFor.lookFor: A verb: it is something you do.

recap: The context of a sentence tells us the meaning of a homonym.
A homonym can be a noun in one sentence and a verb in another, like train.

steps.title: Homonyms that sound different
doThis: Read the two tear sentences aloud: 'A single tear rolled down my cheek' makes the /ear/ sound, and 'If you tear the paper in half' makes the /air/ sound.
Show that read and wound also change: read in the past tense sounds like the colour red, and a wound (an injury) is said differently from wound (winding something up).
Explain that scale, rose, saw and fair sound the same however they are used, while bow, wind, wound, read and tear can be pronounced in different ways.
keyIdeas: Some homonyms are spelt the same, but have contrasting sounds and different meanings (e.g. tear, wind, wound or read).
Unlike many spelling rules, there are no patterns for homonyms and homophones: they are words to learn, with their spelling and meaning in context.
examples: tear: 'A single tear rolled down my cheek' (/ear/ sound) and 'If you tear the paper in half' (/air/ sound).
read: 'She read the instructions carefully before she began' (past tense, sounds like the colour red) and 'I like to read before I go to sleep each night' (present tense).
wound: 'After flying the kite, he carefully wound the string in' (a verb, winding it up) and 'The soldier suffered a serious wound' (a noun, an injury).

checkFor.ask: In 'If you tear the paper in half', does tear make the /ear/ sound or the /air/ sound, and how do we know?
checkFor.lookFor: The /air/ sound. The context (tearing paper in half) tells us which word it is.

recap: Some homonyms are spelt the same but sound different, like tear, wind, wound and read.
Read the whole sentence to find out how to say the word.

steps.title: Curriculum words: community and leisure
doThis: Read the two words: community (a group of people living together) and leisure (free time when not working).
Look at the tricky parts: community has a double m, and leisure has the letters ei in the middle, which is a rare spelling, and ends in s-u-r-e.
Ask the student how they will remember each spelling, for example 'there is sure in leisure'.
keyIdeas: How to spell the curriculum words: community and leisure.

checkFor.ask: What is tricky about spelling community and leisure?
checkFor.lookFor: Community has a double m. Leisure has ei in the middle and ends in s-u-r-e, so there is 'sure' in leisure.

recap: Leisure has ei in the middle and 'sure' at the end: there is sure in leisure.

steps.title: Choose the right homonym
doThis: Read each sentence aloud with a gap and ask the student to choose the right homonym: tear, wound, match, read or rose.
Ask the student which words in the sentence gave the clue, and how the word is said.
Include match in the sense of pairing things up, as in 'match each sentence to the correct answer'.
examples: He wiped a tear away as the train departed.
The doctor used a clean bandage to dress the wound.
The novel was gripping, so I read it in one sitting.
Despite the bad weather, one beautiful rose grew.

checkFor.ask: In 'The novel was gripping, so I ___ it in one sitting', which word fits and how is it said?
checkFor.lookFor: read, said like the colour red, because it is the past tense.

recap: Use the words around the gap to choose the right homonym.
Check the spelling of tear, wound, match, read and rose.

steps.title: Write a whole sentence
doThis: Read the sentence aloud, then ask the student to hold it in their head: picture what is happening, count the words and say it several times out loud.
Ask the student to write it, sounding out each word, looking out for common exception words and checking the punctuation.
Check together: a comma comes after 'time' (after the fronted adverbial) and after 'book' (to separate items in a list).
steps.say: During leisure time, one friend read her book, another trained for a match and a third practised scales on the piano.

checkFor.ask: Which word in the sentence is a curriculum word, and which words are homonyms?
checkFor.lookFor: Leisure is the curriculum word. Homonyms include read, match and scales.

recap: Hold the sentence in your head: picture it, count the words and say it out loud.
Then sound out each word, watch for leisure, and check your punctuation.

steps.title: Try it on your own
doThis: Ask the student to do the lesson quiz on their own. It asks them to match homonyms, homophones and near-homophones to their definitions, to spell tear and community, to give the word class of wound and match, and to pick the sentences that apply to homonyms.
Mark it together and talk through any answer they got wrong.
recap: Do the quiz questions on your own.
Look again at any you got wrong.

steps.title: Recap and finish
doThis: Ask the student to explain what homonyms are and how context helps.

Finish with the summary: homonyms are spelt the same but have different meanings; some also sound different (tear, wind, wound, read); context tells us the meaning and word class; the curriculum words are community and leisure.

checkFor.ask: How do we work out which meaning, and which sound, a homonym has?
checkFor.lookFor: By using the context: the surrounding words and the position of the word in the sentence.

recap: Can you do it now? I can identify the meaning and the correct pronunciation of homonyms based on their context.
Homonyms are spelt the same but mean different things, and the context tells us which meaning it is.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pupils may pronounce homonyms incorrectly in sentences.
commonMistakes.fix: Show that the context of the sentence helps uncover the meaning of the homonym, and therefore its pronunciation: read the whole sentence first, then say the word.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pupils may call words like hear and here homonyms.
commonMistakes.fix: Words that sound the same but are spelt differently are homophones. Only words that are spelt the same as other words, with a different meaning, are homonyms.

watchOut: Give the student a whole sentence and ask which meaning and which sound the homonym has before they write anything: the sentence is the clue.
Read in the past tense sounds like red, the colour, so watch out for that one.
Do not look for a spelling rule: there are no patterns for homonyms and homophones, so each word and its meaning in context has to be learnt.
The quiz also uses the word near-homophones (words that sound similar to other words but have a different spelling), so explain it if the student has not met it.
